plan.angle: Working title: 'Tirzepatide Diarrhea: What's Normal, What Helps' (47 chars). Alternative: 'Tirzepatide Diarrhea: How Common and When It Eases' (50 chars). Keep everything else as planned: Lane A, 8–12 min, the 7 question-named chapters, and the label-exact per-dose rates vs placebo with the trials and population named. Timing goes in as trial averages only: most cases happened during dose escalation, per the label and NEJM 2022 (SURMOUNT-1, adults without diabetes, 72 weeks). Chapter 3 says plainly that the exact cause isn't fully understood. Credit only what the label says (delayed gastric emptying, GI effects), and only what a peer-reviewed review states. Chapter 4 uses the label's AKI and dehydration wording, plus NHS dehydration signs tagged NHS. Chapter 5 uses advisory-tagged habits only where the advisory says them; everything else is an untagged tip. Chapter 6: ask your pharmacist or prescriber, with no products or doses. Chapter 7 uses the label's red flags, with severe stomach pain that won't go away treated as seek-care-now. The don't-stop line becomes 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.' Then 'Not personal advice', then the full prescriber line last. Add the label's oral-contraceptive caveat, the low-blood-sugar caveat for people on insulin or a sulfonylurea, and a kidney-disease 'get advice early' line. Use 'your local urgent care or emergency number'. The ending line, the line-1 Watch next link to Side Effects, the beat-sync diff and the state-change thumbnail stay as planned ('Gut Calming Down', calm tummy character, no body imagery).
plan.why:
#3 in the playbook's queue of new tirzepatide long-forms, and nothing about the dropped beat-sync failure carries over. It's one of the most common label side effects, it's verifiable almost entirely from the current Zepbound label plus NEJM and NHS, it sits right next to Side Effects (our best source of suggested-video traffic) and Constipation, and it doesn't overlap today's Shorts (eyes, blood pressure, injection sites). | fact-check: The topic is safe, evergreen, well sourced and on strategy for Lane A. The Zepbound and Mounjaro labels report diarrhea for each dose against placebo, and say most GI events happened during dose escalation. NEJM 2022 (SURMOUNT-1) reports per-arm GI rates and says they were mostly mild to moderate. None of this is misinformation bait or strike risk.

Why modify:
(1) The working title 'Why It Happens' promises an explanation, but chapter 3 has to admit the exact cause isn't fully understood. That's a hook the content can't fully pay off, so lead with what the video does deliver (how common it is and what helps). Alternatively, keep 'why' only if chapter 3 states plainly what's known (slowed gastric emptying and GI effects in the label, timing tied to dose increases) and what isn't.
(2) The prescribed first sentence must use the label's or paper's exact wording. Don't add 'mostly mild to moderate' unless the source cited for it says that (the NEJM paper does; check whether the label says it). Both statements need a source tag and must be presented as trial averages.
(3) Chapter 7 lists severe stomach pain that won't go away, which is a pancreatitis warning where the label says to stop and seek care. Scope the don't-stop line to fit: 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.'
(4) Add a short caveat from the label: tirzepatide may reduce how well birth control pills work, for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase. Use the label's exact wording. Don't add our own claim that diarrhea itself affects pill absorption unless a source tag supports it.
(5) If the script mentions eating less or skipping meals while unwell, add the low-blood-sugar caveat for people on insulin or a sulfonylurea, and tell them to talk to their prescriber.
(6) Chapter 6 stays generic: ask your pharmacist or prescriber, with no product names or doses. Add a line that people with kidney disease should get advice early, since dehydration plus AKI risk matters most for them.
(7) Report diarrhea rates for each dose exactly as printed, never pooled. Say which label is used: Zepbound for weight management, Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes. Don't mix the two populations in one number.
(8) Confirm that the ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS 2025 advisory actually contains GI-symptom guidance before giving it a source tag. If it doesn't, tag those habits as our own tips with no source.

package.description:
Quick answer: In Zepbound's weight-management trials, diarrhea was reported by 19% on tirzepatide 5 mg, 21% on 10 mg and 23% on 15 mg, vs 7% on placebo, mostly during dose escalation, decreasing over time. Mounjaro's type 2 diabetes trials had lower rates, still above placebo.

Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea may lead to dehydration, which if severe could cause acute kidney injury. Tell your prescriber if stomach problems are severe or won't go away. Severe stomach pain that won't go away: the label says stop and call your healthcare provider right away. Serious allergic reaction: stop and get medical help right away. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.working_title: Tirzepatide Diarrhea: What's Normal, What Helps
script.hook_pattern: Direct answer to the title, then a visceral 'you' scenario (the sudden dash to the bathroom after a dose increase), plus two open loops: a pharmacology detail in the label (paid off in chapter 3) and the one exception to 'don't stop on your own' (paid off in chapter 7)

scenes.narration: Diarrhea is one of the more common side effects of tirzepatide. In the trials, most reports happened while the dose was being increased, and they decreased over time.

visual.stock_query: calm tummy character on a gentle ramp

scenes.retention_device: First sentence answers the title directly

scenes.narration: Picture this. You're three days past a dose increase. You're at work, and your stomach suddenly has opinions. You're quietly working out where the nearest bathroom is.

visual.stock_query: worried office worker eyeing bathroom sign

scenes.narration: Imagine Jo, fifty-one, who's just been through exactly that. Her first thought is: is this normal, or is something wrong? Her second thought: is this my life now?

visual.stock_query: worried woman at kitchen table evening

scenes.narration: If that's been you, you're not alone, and it doesn't mean you're doing something wrong. In the weight-management trials, about one in five people on the five milligram dose reported diarrhea.

visual.stock_query: five friends one holding stomach kindly

scenes.narration: In the next few minutes, you'll get the exact numbers for each dose, the timing pattern from the trials, what may help, and how to tell normal from call-today.
scenes.retention_device: Promise of what the viewer will get

scenes.narration: And stay for one detail tucked into the label's pharmacology section. It helps explain why the first weeks after a change can feel different from later ones.
Plus, there's one situation where the usual rule about not stopping on your own flips. We'll get there. Quick note first: this is general information, not personal advice.

visual.stock_query: Medi mascot holding info sign calmly

scenes.narration: Chapter one. How common is it, really?

visual.stock_query: teal title card with tummy icon

scenes.narration: Let's go straight to the Zepbound label, which covers weight management. Its numbers come from placebo-controlled trials in adults with obesity or overweight.
On the five milligram dose of tirzepatide, nineteen percent of people reported diarrhea.
On ten milligrams, twenty-one percent. On fifteen milligrams, twenty-three percent.
And here's the number people skip. On placebo, an injection with no medicine in it, seven percent reported diarrhea too.
So some of those bathroom trips would have happened anyway. Food, stress and stomach bugs don't pause for a clinical trial. The extra risk linked to the medicine is the gap between the two numbers.
scenes.retention_device: Reframe that changes how they read stats

scenes.narration: Put it in people. On fifteen milligrams, that's roughly twenty-three people out of a hundred, compared with seven out of a hundred on placebo.
Notice the pattern, too. The rate rises a little with each higher dose, from nineteen, to twenty-one, to twenty-three percent.
Now, if you have type 2 diabetes and take Mounjaro, check the Mounjaro label instead. Its numbers come from different trials, in adults with type 2 diabetes.

visual.stock_query: two different medicine leaflets side by side

scenes.narration: In those trials, diarrhea rates were lower than in the Zepbound weight trials, but still higher than placebo at every dose.
These are separate trials in separate groups of people, so don't blend them into one number. Read the label that matches your prescription.

visual.fact: Each label reports its own trials and population

scenes.narration: But a percentage only tells you how many. It doesn't tell you when. And the when is where this gets much more useful.
Chapter two. When is it most likely?

visual.stock_query: teal title card with calendar icon

scenes.narration: Here's the timing, as trial averages. The Zepbound label says the majority of reports of nausea, vomiting and diarrhea happened during dose escalation, and decreased over time.
Dose escalation just means the stretch when the dose is being stepped up. In the big weight trial, SURMOUNT-1, that was a gradual climb over several weeks before people reached their assigned dose.
SURMOUNT-1 followed two thousand, five hundred and thirty-nine adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and without diabetes, for seventy-two weeks.

visual.stock_query: large group of diverse cartoon adults

scenes.narration: The researchers reported that the gut side effects were mostly mild to moderate, and happened mainly during dose escalation.
So think of it like a ramp, not a cliff. On average, these side effects bunched up around the dose increases, then eased.
Back to Jo. Her diarrhea started a few days after her dose went up, which fits the trial pattern. It doesn't mean hers will fade on a set schedule. But it's a reason for patience, not panic.

visual.stock_query: woman taking a calm deep breath

scenes.narration: One more number. In SURMOUNT-1, between about four and seven in a hundred people on tirzepatide stopped because of side effects of any kind, compared with about three in a hundred on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Stopped for any side effect, tirzepatide

scenes.narration: So most people kept going. But that raises a fair question. Why would a medicine that works on appetite affect your bowels at all?

visual.stock_query: curious cartoon gut with question mark

scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer before section change

scenes.narration: Chapter three. Why might it happen?

visual.stock_query: teal title card with stomach icon

scenes.narration: Honest answer first. The exact reason some people get diarrhea on tirzepatide isn't fully understood. The label doesn't name a single cause.
Here's what the label does say. Tirzepatide acts on two hormone receptors, called GIP and GLP-1.

visual.stock_query: two friendly keys fitting two locks

scenes.narration: It also delays gastric emptying. In plain words, food leaves your stomach more slowly than usual.
And here's the detail I promised. The label says that delay is largest after the first dose, and the effect diminishes over time.
That doesn't prove it's what causes diarrhea. But it shows your gut's response to this medicine changes over time, which fits the timing pattern from the trials.
The label groups diarrhea with other gut reactions, like nausea, vomiting and constipation. And it notes these can sometimes be severe.
There's a practical angle, too. When your appetite changes, what and how you eat often changes with it. That isn't a proven cause, but it's something you can actually work with.
But before we get to food, there's one thing that matters more than any eating tip. It's what diarrhea can quietly take from you.
Chapter four. Why does hydration matter?

visual.stock_query: teal title card with water drop

scenes.narration: Diarrhea means losing fluid. The label is direct about it. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea may lead to dehydration, which if severe could cause acute kidney injury.
So this isn't only about inconvenience. The label advises taking precautions to avoid losing too much fluid.

visual.myth: A bit of diarrhea is just inconvenient
visual.fact: The label warns fluid loss can affect kidneys

scenes.narration: How do you know you're running low? The NHS lists signs like feeling thirsty, and dark yellow, strong-smelling pee.
Others include peeing less often than usual, feeling dizzy or lightheaded, feeling tired, a dry mouth, lips and tongue, and sunken eyes.
The NHS also suggests that if you feel sick, small sips are easier than big gulps.
scenes.on_screen_text: Small sips if you feel sick

scenes.narration: A simple habit: keep a glass or bottle within reach, and notice your pee colour through the day. Paler is what you're aiming for.

If you have kidney disease, this matters even more. The label says to monitor kidney function in people with kidney problems who report severe gut side effects. So get advice early, not after days of symptoms.
Jo, by the way, noticed she'd been drinking less, because she didn't want more bathroom trips. Very human. And exactly backwards.
So, fluids first. Now, what about food? Some habits may help, and one of them is about speed, not ingredients.
scenes.retention_device: New open loop into next chapter

scenes.narration: Chapter five. What eating habits may help?

visual.stock_query: teal title card with plate icon

scenes.narration: These are practical tips, not trial results. They weren't tested in the tirzepatide trials. But they're gentle, low-risk, and easy to try.
Tip one: smaller portions. With food leaving your stomach more slowly, a big meal can sit heavy. Smaller plates, more often if you need, may feel easier.
Tip two, the one about speed: slow down. Put your fork down between bites, and stop when you feel comfortably full, not stuffed.
Tip three: go easy on very greasy, fried or rich foods while your gut settles. If you notice they make things worse, that's useful information.

visual.stock_query: fried food plate with pause sign

scenes.narration: Tip four: learn your own triggers. For some people it might be spicy food, lots of caffeine, alcohol, or sugar-free sweets.
Tip five: plain, gentle foods on rough days. Think toast, rice, bananas, soup, or whatever simple foods sit well with you. And keep some protein in, in gentle forms like eggs, soft fish or tofu.
So: smaller portions, slower bites, easy on greasy, know your triggers, and gentle foods on rough days.
One important caveat. The label says the risk of low blood sugar may be higher when tirzepatide is used with insulin or a sulfonylurea.
scenes.on_screen_text: Insulin or sulfonylurea? Low sugar risk

scenes.narration: So if you take one of those, and you're eating much less or skipping meals because of diarrhea, talk to your prescriber.
scenes.on_screen_text: Eating much less? Tell your prescriber

scenes.narration: And if you use birth control pills, there's a separate label caveat. Tirzepatide may reduce the efficacy of oral hormonal contraceptives, because of delayed gastric emptying.
The label advises using a non-oral method, or adding a barrier method, for four weeks after starting, and for four weeks after each dose increase. Ask your prescriber what fits you.
scenes.on_screen_text: 4 weeks after start and each increase

scenes.narration: Everything so far, you can do at home. But some things go better with a quick question to someone who knows your medicines.
Chapter six. Who can I ask?

visual.stock_query: teal title card with speech bubble

scenes.narration: Your pharmacist is one of the most underused people in healthcare. They can look at your whole medicine list, often without an appointment.
Before taking anything for diarrhea, including over-the-counter remedies, ask your pharmacist or prescriber whether it's right for you alongside tirzepatide and your other medicines.
Good questions to bring. Is this level of diarrhea expected for me? How much should I be drinking? Is there anything I should avoid? And when should I call you?
Picture Jo's pharmacist asking how many days it's been, and whether she's keeping fluids down. Simple questions, but they're the ones that sort normal from not.
And tell your prescriber about side effects that bother you, even if they seem small. They can't help with what they don't hear about.
Which brings us to the most important part of this video. Because a few symptoms aren't wait and see. They're get help now.
scenes.on_screen_text: Wait and see, or get help?

scenes.narration: Chapter seven. When should I call?

visual.stock_query: teal title card with phone icon

scenes.narration: First, the label says to tell your healthcare provider if you have stomach problems that are severe or will not go away.
Get advice, too, if you have signs of dehydration, like peeing much less or feeling dizzy, or if you keep being sick and can't keep fluids down.
The NHS adds that bloody diarrhea, or diarrhea lasting more than seven days, needs urgent medical advice.

Now the seek-care-now signs. The label warns about pancreatitis: severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting. You may feel the pain from your stomach to your back.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe pain that won't go away

visual.stock_query: calm neutral mascot with alert sign

scenes.narration: The label also lists gallbladder warning signs, like pain in your upper stomach, fever, yellowing of your skin or eyes, or clay-coloured stools.

And signs of a serious allergic reaction: swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing or swallowing, a severe rash or itching, fainting or feeling dizzy, or a very rapid heartbeat.

items: Face, lips, tongue or throat swelling

scenes.narration: For those pancreatitis signs, the label says to stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away. For a serious allergic reaction, stop and get medical help right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Label says: stop and get help

scenes.narration: If it feels like an emergency, contact your local urgent care or emergency number. These signs are the exception the label itself makes to the usual rule.
scenes.on_screen_text: Local urgent care or emergency number

scenes.narration: And Jo? In our story, her symptoms settle over the following weeks. That's the pattern the trial averages describe, though everyone is different. What changed most was that she stopped feeling scared, because she knew what to watch for.

Here's your checklist. Read the label that matches your prescription. Expect that side effects may bunch up around dose increases. Sip fluids and watch for dehydration signs. Eat smaller, slower, gentler meals. And know your red flags.
For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.
scenes.on_screen_text: Don't switch, stop or change on your own

visual.stock_query: calm neutral mascot with info card

scenes.narration: Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
scenes.on_screen_text: Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
This script is accurate and safe to ship once the four minor fixes below are made. Nothing in it would mislead a viewer.

Checked against the sources:
- **Zepbound diarrhea rates** (S1) match the weight-management trial table: 19%, 21% and 23% on 5, 10 and 15 mg, against 7% on placebo.
- **Zepbound label wording** (S1) matches:
  - most nausea, vomiting and diarrhea happened during dose escalation and decreased over time
  - tirzepatide acts on GIP and GLP-1 receptors and delays gastric emptying, and that delay is largest after the first dose and then diminishes
  - GI reactions are sometimes severe
  - dehydration can lead to acute kidney injury, so take precautions, and monitor kidney function in people with kidney problems who report severe GI reactions
  - low blood sugar risk is higher with insulin or a sulfonylurea
  - for oral contraceptives, use a non-oral or barrier method for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase
- **Medication Guide wording** for pancreatitis, gallbladder, serious allergic reaction and "severe or will not go away" also matches.
- **Mounjaro** (S2): diarrhea rates in the type 2 diabetes trials are lower than Zepbound's but above placebo at every dose. The script correctly says not to blend the two.
- **SURMOUNT-1** (S3): 2,539 adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes, followed for 72 weeks. GI effects were mostly mild to moderate and mainly during dose escalation. Stopping for side effects was 4.3–7.1% on tirzepatide vs 2.6% on placebo, so "about 4–7 vs about 3 in 100" is fair.
- **NHS pages** (S4, S5): the dehydration signs, "small sips if you feel sick", and the 111-now advice for bloody diarrhoea, diarrhoea over 7 days or not keeping fluids down are all confirmed.

Safety and framing are handled well:
- the kidney disease caveat, the insulin/sulfonylurea caveat and the birth control caveat are all there
- the "don't stop" line is limited to cases that aren't emergencies, and the label's own "stop and get help" cases are named
- the help line works in all four markets
- eating tips are clearly labelled as untested
- Jo is clearly marked as hypothetical
- the label wording is tied to the gut effect without claiming it causes diarrhea

All four issues are minor. Two source dates in the list are wrong, one safety line on screen is cut short, one stat on screen is missing its comparison, and two scenes are tagged to sources that don't say that part.

I could reach both label PDFs and the PubMed record but couldn't extract their text. The label wording and figures above are confirmed from my own knowledge of the labels and the NEJM paper, not from text pulled on this run. The S1 "28 Aug 2026" and S2 "2026 revision" dates come from your craft notes. The NHS figures and dates were read from the live pages.

thumbnail.reasoning:
All three are clean, on-brand, legible renders with a single labeled mascot and good contrast. Candidate #0 ("GUT CALMING DOWN") best fits the proven state-change pattern (worried gray gut → calm green gut) that the playbook flags as the top-performing thumbnail style (Side Effects 4.04% CTR).
